**Holding.** Yes, they have the privilege. Sec. 7 of the Military Commissions Act, which stripped federal courts of jurisdiction over their habeas petitions, operates as an unconstitutional suspension of the writ, and the review procedures of the Detainee Treatment Act are not an adequate substitute.

**Question.** Whether foreign nationals detained at Guantanamo Bay have the constitutional privilege of habeas corpus, and whether the Military Commissions Act could remove it.

## Why it matters

The Court struck down a provision Congress had enacted in response to its own earlier ruling in [Hamdan](../cases/hamdan-2006.qmd), and, as Justice Scalia's dissent put it, for the first time extended constitutional habeas to noncitizens held by the military abroad. It opened years of habeas litigation in federal court in Washington, which, rather than new legislation, defined the detention standard in practice.

## Status

Good law.

## Statutes at issue

- [Military Commissions Act](../statutes/mil-commissions-2006.qmd){.subj}. Struck down Sec. 7, which barred habeas petitions from Guantanamo detainees.
- [Detainee Treatment Act](../statutes/dta-2005.qmd){.subj}. Held its review procedures were not an adequate substitute for habeas corpus.

Studied in [Unit 3: Deciding to use force](../study/units/war-powers.qmd).
